en.page_title: Case Study: Warehouse & Inventory Subsystem (WMS) - Bowei Xu
en.page_description: How I built the warehouse half of an internal operations platform: shared-schema stock tracking, receiving workflows, lot-level traceability, and scan-driven shop-floor counts.
en.title: Warehouse & Inventory Subsystem (WMS)
en.disclaimer: A sanitized write-up of the warehouse and shop-floor half of the internal operations platform I designed and built as the sole developer at Fuel Cell Store. It runs on the same database as the order-to-shipment half, which has its own write-up. Product details and proprietary code are omitted; what follows is architecture and engineering decisions.
en.related: Read the order-to-shipment half of this platform

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: Manufacturing needed real-time inventory that the storefront and accounting tools could not provide. Counts drifted, and nothing recorded who pulled what against which work order. The materials themselves vary widely: some track cleanly by discrete lot, others are roll goods and liquids that resist exact measurement.

As the sole developer, I built this half in two parts. The first tracks everyday stock, receiving, builds, waste, and physical counts. The second handles the one category of material that does track by lot number and exact quantity, a ground-up rebuild of an older system that had become unreliable and hard to maintain. Both run on the same internal Ubuntu Linux server as the rest of the platform.

sections.heading: Scope
list: Stock and SKUs: real-time quantities, pulling against work orders, and manual adjustments
Receiving: purchase orders moving through pending, partially arrived, and arrived, feeding stock on arrival
Builds and bill-of-materials: assembly tracking and per-build material consumption
Physical counts: QR-scanned counts compared against the database, with discrepancy reporting
Waste: scrap recorded against stock, with its own audit trail
Lot-tracked materials subsystem: lot-level inventory, weekly snapshots, and threshold alerts
Reporting and analytics: stock trends, purchase-versus-usage, low-stock and reconciliation reports
QR codes: bulk generation, plus shop-floor scanning for stock, lots, and operator badges

sections.heading: Architecture
paragraphs: Two server-rendered PHP applications on Microsoft SQL Server, where every page is either a screen or a JSON endpoint. The main system shares the ERP's database; the lot-tracked-materials subsystem has its own on the same server.

tiers.label: PHP
tiers.desc: UI pages, JSON endpoints, cron jobs

tiers.label: SQL Server
items: main database, shared with the ERP
materials database, owned by the subsystem

architecture.aria: Architecture diagram: the browser talks over the internal network to a single Ubuntu Linux server running PHP and SQL Server.

paragraphs_after: Why two systems rather than one? The main one grew alongside the ERP and shares its tables, so reads and writes are immediate and there is no API layer to keep in sync. The materials subsystem got its own database because that data needs tighter access control, lot-level precision, and separate alerting. Isolating it also let me retire the legacy version without putting live inventory at risk.

Neither application uses a framework. With one person maintaining both, a page that is a single file is the fastest thing to open, understand, and change months later, and deploying stays a file copy onto the server already running the ERP. The cost is that auth and input validation live in shared includes rather than middleware, which is the first thing I would change if a second maintainer joined.

sections.heading: Scale
list: 20 to 30 internal users across the office and the shop floor at the same time
Stock lookups and inventory reports return in under a second

subsections.title: 1. Cross-system work order locking
subsections.body: Two operators pulling against the same work order would corrupt stock counts, and the ERP could check that order out at the same time. Scanning a work order takes a short-lived lock in a shared table. Saving releases it, leaving the page releases it, and a scheduled job clears anything older than five minutes. Because the table is shared, the ERP refuses to check out a work order the shop floor has locked, so the conflict is settled between the two systems rather than inside either one.

subsections.title: 2. Shop-floor workflows driven by scanning
subsections.body: Operators scan instead of typing. A badge identifies the operator, a work order is validated and locked on scan, and SKUs and material lots are identified the same way. Both input paths work: a hardware barcode gun types into the focused field, and the browser scans through the camera when no gun is at hand. On a shop floor, typing is where the errors come from.

subsections.title: 3. Two material sources, reconciled rather than auto-synced
subsections.body: Usage of these lot-tracked materials gets recorded in two places: the materials subsystem and the build-itemization flow in the main system. Only one of them owns the actual quantity deduction; the other is read-only reference, matched on a normalized work-order-and-lot key. Reconciliation reports list the rows that exist in one source but not the other. I left automatic dual writes out on purpose, because without a clear owner they hide quantity drift instead of correcting it. Closing a gap stays a decision someone makes, not something the system does quietly.

subsections.title: 4. Discrepancy lock to stop drift
subsections.body: When a physical count does not match the database, the SKU is flagged and pulling against it is blocked until the variance is resolved, and filing the discrepancy notifies the admins. A quantity already known to be wrong stops moving while someone looks into it.

subsections.title: 5. Audit trail and historical snapshots
subsections.body: Every state-changing operation records who did it, what changed, and the before and after values, all in one audit table. A scheduled job snapshots stock levels into a separate table on a fixed interval, and the trend charts read that snapshot, so reporting never competes with live operations.

sections.heading: Results
list: Replaced drifting spreadsheet counts with real-time inventory across stock, receiving, builds, waste, and lot-tracked materials
Gave the shop floor a scan-driven workflow for pulling, receiving, and counting, with every movement on the audit trail
Prevented concurrent-edit and cross-system conflicts through work-order locking shared with the ERP
Built and shipped both systems single-handedly, and kept them running in production

zh.page_title: 案例研究：仓储与库存子系统（WMS） - 徐博伟
zh.page_description: 我如何构建企业内部运营平台的仓储一侧：共库共表的库存跟踪、收货流程、批次级物料追溯，以及扫码驱动的车间盘点。
zh.title: 仓储与库存子系统（WMS）
zh.disclaimer: 脱敏案例分析。我在 Fuel Cell Store 作为唯一开发者，设计并构建了内部运营平台中仓储与车间的这一半；它和从下单到发货的另一半共用同一个数据库，那一半另有独立案例。产品细节与专有代码已省略，这里只谈架构和工程决策。
zh.related: 查看这套平台从下单到发货的部分

sections.heading: 背景
paragraphs: 生产需要实时准确的库存，而商城和财务工具给不了。账面数字经常对不上，谁为哪张工单领了什么也没有记录。物料本身差别还很大：有的能按批号一一对上，有的是卷材、液体，本来就称不准。
作为唯一开发者，我把这一半拆成两部分来做。第一部分管日常库存、收货、装配、报废和实物盘点。第二部分专门处理那一类能按批号和精确数量记清楚的物料，是把一套已经不可靠、也难以维护的老系统彻底重写。两者和平台其余部分跑在同一台内部 Ubuntu Linux 服务器上。

sections.heading: 范围
list: 库存与 SKU：实时数量、按工单领料、人工调整
收货：采购订单在待到货、部分到货、已到货之间流转，到货即计入库存
装配与物料清单：装配追踪，以及每次装配的物料消耗
实物盘点：扫码清点后与数据库比对，差异单独记录
报废：报废计入库存，单独留痕
物料子系统：按批号管理库存、每周快照、阈值告警
报表与分析：库存趋势、采购对比用量、低库存与对账报表
QR 码：批量生成，车间扫描库存、批号和操作员工牌

sections.heading: 架构
paragraphs: 两套服务端渲染的 PHP 应用，数据库都是 Microsoft SQL Server，每个页面要么是一个界面，要么是一个 JSON 接口。主系统直接和 ERP 共用数据库，物料子系统在同一台服务器上另有一个自己的库。

client.label: 浏览器
client.desc: 服务端渲染页面、QR 扫描

architecture.host: 单台 Ubuntu Linux 服务器

tiers.label: PHP
tiers.desc: 界面页面、JSON 接口、定时任务

tiers.label: SQL Server
items: 主数据库，与 ERP 共用
物料数据库，由子系统独占

architecture.aria: 架构图：浏览器通过内部网络访问单台 Ubuntu Linux 服务器，服务器上运行 PHP 与 SQL Server。

paragraphs_after: 为什么是两套而不是一套？主系统是跟着 ERP 一起长出来的，和它共用数据表，读写都是即时的，也就没有 API 层要维护。物料子系统单独建库，是因为这类数据需要更严的权限、批号级的精度和自己的告警；把它隔开，我才能在不动线上库存的前提下把旧系统换掉。
两套应用都不用框架。一个人同时维护两套系统，一个页面就是一个文件，几个月后重新打开、看懂、改掉都是最快的；部署也一直只是往那台已经跑着 ERP 的服务器上拷文件。代价是鉴权和输入校验只能放在共享的 include 里，而不是中间件——如果有第二个人接手，这是最先要动的地方。

sections.heading: 规模
list: 办公室与车间合计 20 到 30 名内部用户同时在线
库存查询和库存报表都在 1 秒内返回

subsections.title: 1. 跨系统的工单锁
subsections.body: 两名操作员同时对同一张工单领料会把库存数搞乱，而 ERP 也可能在同一时刻签出这张工单。扫工单时会在一张共享表里拿一把短时锁：保存时释放，离开页面时释放，定时任务清掉任何超过五分钟的锁。因为这张表是共享的，车间锁住的工单 ERP 签不出去——冲突在两套系统之间解决，而不是各自为政。

subsections.title: 2. 以扫码驱动的车间流程
subsections.body: 操作员靠扫码，不靠打字。扫工牌确认身份，扫工单完成校验并加锁，SKU 和物料批号同样靠扫。两种扫码方式都支持：硬件条码枪直接把内容打进聚焦的输入框，手边没有枪时用浏览器调摄像头扫。在车间，错误基本都出在打字上。

subsections.title: 3. 两个物料来源，用对账而非自动同步
subsections.body: 这类物料的用量有两个记录入口：物料子系统，和主系统里的装配拆料流程。真正的数量扣减只归其中一方，另一方是只读参考，两边按归一化后的“工单 + 批号”对上。对账报表专门列出只在一边存在的记录。双写是我故意没做的：没有明确的归属方，双写只会把数量漂移盖住，而不是纠正它。要不要补平这个差，始终是人做的决定，而不是系统悄悄替你做。

subsections.title: 4. 用差异锁阻止漂移
subsections.body: 实物盘点和数据库对不上时，这个 SKU 会被标记，在差异解决前不许再领料，提交差异的同时自动通知管理员。一个已知是错的数量，先停下来，不要在调查期间继续漂。

subsections.title: 5. 审计记录与历史快照
subsections.body: 每一次改变状态的操作，都会把操作者、改了什么、改动前后的值记进同一张审计表。定时任务按固定周期把库存水平快照到另一张表，趋势图读的是快照，所以报表不会和线上操作抢资源。

sections.heading: 成果
list: 用实时库存取代了不断漂移的表格数字，覆盖库存、收货、装配、报废和按批号管理的物料
让车间的领料、收货、盘点都由扫码驱动，每一次库存变动都有留痕
通过与 ERP 共享工单锁，避免了并发编辑和跨系统冲突
两套系统由我一人构建交付，并在生产环境持续运行
